key_features.classic_presentation: Acute pancreatitis presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, often described as boring or penetrating. Pain develops rapidly over hours. Nausea and vomiting are prominent. Patient often leans forward for relief.
key_features.typical_demographics: Most common causes: gallstones (40%) and alcohol (30%). Can occur at any age but peak 40-60 years. Male predominance in alcoholic pancreatitis.
key_features.pathophysiology_brief: Premature activation of pancreatic enzymes leads to autodigestion of pancreas, inflammation, and systemic complications.

diagnostic_questions.context: Epigastric location is classic. Pain is midline or slightly left of midline.
Radiation to back is highly specific for pancreatitis (70-80%). Described as 'boring' or 'penetrating' through.
Pancreatitis pain is typically severe (8-10/10) and constant. One of the most painful conditions.
Leaning forward or fetal position often provides some relief. Lying supine worsens pain.
Nausea and vomiting present in >90% of cases. Often severe and persistent.
Gallstones and alcohol account for 70% of cases. Ask specifically about recent alcohol consumption.
Onset typically over 1-6 hours. Reaches maximum intensity quickly.
Low-grade fever common. High fever suggests necrotizing pancreatitis or infected necrosis.

differential_diagnosis.key_difference: Sudden onset, rigid abdomen, free air on imaging
RUQ (not epigastric), Murphy's sign, no back radiation
Pain out of proportion to exam, older age, vascular disease

red_flags.action: Severe pancreatitis with shock - ICU level care needed
Possible perforation or necrotizing pancreatitis - surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Bluish discoloration around umbilicus (Cullen's sign) or flanks (Grey Turner's sign)

typical_management: NPO, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, pain control, monitor for complications. Mild pancreatitis: supportive care, usually resolves in 3-7 days. Severe: ICU monitoring, may require intervention.
disposition: Emergency department for evaluation. Mild cases: admission for supportive care. Severe: ICU admission.
patient_education: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas. It requires immediate medical care and hospitalization. Treatment focuses on rest, fluids, and pain control while the pancreas heals. Severe cases can be life-threatening.
